She slid three copies across the table. Daniel took his. Lucia took hers. Rosa looked at hers for a moment without touching it, then drew it toward her with two fingers, as if testing whether it was hot.

They read.

Asha watched them read without watching them read. She had learned, early, the trick of looking at a document on the table in front of her while taking in, peripherally, the faces of the people around it. Daniel read fast. He had always read fast, she suspected, and he was reading fast now partly out of habit and partly out of the need to be seen reading fast, to be the first one finished, to retain some small primacy in a room in which his primacy had been considerably reduced. Lucia read slowly, going back over phrases, her lips moving very faintly on the technical terms. Rosa read at the pace of a woman who had not been asked, often, to read formal English, and who was not embarrassed by her pace but who was conserving herself, taking the words one at a time, deciding about each one.

Daniel finished first. He set the memorandum down. He did not speak. He waited. Asha noted, with a small flicker of professional approval she did not let show, that he had learned something yesterday and was using it today.

Lucia finished second. She looked up at Asha and nodded once.

Rosa took another four minutes. When she reached the end she went back to the beginning and read the first paragraph again. Then she folded her hands on top of the memorandum and looked at Asha.

\"I have a question,\" she said.

\"Please.\"

\"The right of first refusal. If I wanted to keep the house — I am only asking. I do not say that I do. If I wanted to keep the house, I would have to pay the other two for their shares.\"

\"Yes.\"

\"At fair market value.\"

\"As established by the appraisal, yes.\"

\"Which would be a number I cannot pay.\"

\"It might be,\" Asha said carefully. \"It depends on the appraisal, on the financing options available to you, on whether the other beneficiaries are willing to accept a payment over time secured by the property itself. There are configurations in which it would be possible. There are configurations in which it would not. I cannot tell you today which configuration applies.\"

\"All right.\"

\"Ms. Maldonado.\"

\"Yes.\"

\"You do not have to decide today whether you want to keep the house. You have to decide today only whether you are willing to find out what would be required.\"

Rosa looked at her for a long moment.

\"I am willing,\" she said, \"to find out.\"

\"Thank you.\"

Daniel cleared his throat.

\"I have a question,\" he said.

\"Please.\"

\"If — \" He stopped. He started over. \"If Rosa wants to keep the house. And if the appraisal comes in at a number she cannot pay outright. And if Lucia and I were to — were to be willing to accept a payment over time. The memorandum says secured by the property itself. Does that mean a mortgage. From her to us.\"

\"In effect, yes. A purchase-money obligation, secured by the house, payable on terms the three of you would negotiate.\"

\"At what interest rate.\"

\"At whatever rate the three of you agree.\"

\"It could be zero.\"

\"It could be zero. It could also be the applicable federal rate. It could be anything in between. The IRS has views about very low rates among related parties, but you are not, in the technical sense, related parties, and even where the views apply they are manageable. We would structure it carefully.\"

Daniel was quiet. He looked at the memorandum. He looked at Rosa. He looked at his sister. He looked, finally, back at the memorandum.

\"I am not saying,\" he said, \"that I would agree to that.\"

\"You don't have to say that today.\"

\"I am saying that I would consider it.\"

title: === SCENE 9 ===
content:
=== SCENE 9 ===
Lucia made a small noise. It was not a laugh and not a sound of contempt. It was the sound of a woman who had not expected her brother to say what he had just said, and who was making, in real time, an adjustment to a story she had been telling herself about him for many years, and who did not yet know whether the adjustment was permanent or whether it was an artifact of grief and would not survive the week.

\"Daniel,\" she said.

\"Don't.\"

\"I wasn't going to — \"

\"Don't, Lucia.\"

\"All right.\"

He put his hand flat on the memorandum. He looked at Asha.

\"What do you need from us today,\" he said.

\"I need you to agree to the appraisal. I have three names of independent appraisers. Any one of them is acceptable to my office and to the Register of Wills. I would like you to choose one by the end of business today. I will arrange the inspection. The report should be available within ten days. We will meet again on the day the report is delivered. Between now and then I would like the three of you to live in this house, or visit this house, or stay out of this house, as you each prefer, and to refrain from removing any item from the premises without notice to the other two and to my office.\"

\"Including — \"

\"Including objects you believe to be personally yours. Including objects of sentimental rather than financial value. Including, Mr. Serrano, the watch in the upstairs study that I noticed yesterday you were looking at while we spoke about the dining room.\"

Daniel went very still.

\"It was my grandfather's,\" he said.

\"Then it will, in all likelihood, be yours. But it will be yours by agreement among the three of you, recorded in the inventory, and not by removal in the meantime. I am asking this of all of you. I am not singling you out. Ms. Serrano, the same applies to the letter, which I would like you to leave in the sewing room where you found it for the remainder of the inventory period, after which it is, in my view as your attorney, indisputably yours. Ms. Maldonado, the same applies to the books in the second-floor hallway.\"

Rosa looked up sharply.

\"How did you know,\" she said.

\"You were looking at them yesterday when we came down from the sewing room.\"

\"Ah.\"

\"They were a gift to you. I would not be surprised to learn that they were inscribed.\"

\"They are inscribed.\"

\"Then they are, in all likelihood, yours, by the same logic. But they will be yours by agreement and not by removal in the meantime.\"

\"Yes,\" Rosa said. \"I understand.\"

\"Thank you.\"

They chose the appraiser. Daniel suggested the one whose name he recognized from a real-estate transaction he had handled at his firm; Lucia objected on principle; Rosa, asked her opinion, said she had no opinion about appraisers but that she trusted the counselor to know who was honest, and the counselor said any of the three names was honest, and they took the second name on the list, which was a woman named Beverly Ostrowski who had appraised the house across the street the previous spring and was, by Rosa's recollection of neighborhood gossip, fair.

By eleven they were done with the formal work of the morning. Asha closed her folder. She did not yet stand up.

\"There is one more thing,\" she said, \"that I would like to say, and then I will leave you to your morning. It is not legal advice. It is a request.\"

The three of them looked at her.

\"You are now,\" she said, \"the co-owners of a building. You are also, separately and not by my doing and not by anything that will appear in the file, the three people who loved your mother most closely in the last decade of her life. Those two facts are going to be in tension over the next two weeks. The legal frame I have given you is designed to keep that tension productive. It is not designed to resolve it. It cannot resolve it. The resolution will happen, if it happens, in this room, without me, and possibly without any document at all. I would like to ask each of you — and I am asking this as a person who has watched many families do this badly and a few do it well — to give each other, for the next two weeks, the benefit of a doubt you do not yet feel like extending. That is all. I will not say it again.\"

She stood up.

\"I will see myself out,\" she said. \"The memorandum is on the table. The appraiser will call this afternoon to arrange access. Please call my office if anything arises.\"

She picked up her bag. She walked to the dining room door. She had her hand on the doorframe when Daniel said her name.

\"Counselor.\"

She turned.

\"Yes.\"

He was standing now. He had pushed his chair back. He looked, in the dining room light, less rehearsed than she had ever seen him.

\"I want to ask you something,\" he said, \"and I want you to answer it as my attorney and not as — not as anything else. Because I don't know who to ask.\"

\"I am not your attorney, Mr. Serrano. I am the attorney for the estate. There is a difference.\"

\"I know there is a difference. Answer me as the attorney for the estate.\"

\"All right.\"

\"Should I get my own lawyer.\"

Lucia made another small noise, different from the first.

Asha considered the question. She considered it with the care it deserved, which was considerable, because the answer would shape the next two weeks and possibly the rest of the family's relationship with itself, and because the question, asked in this room in front of his sister and the housekeeper, was either a piece of late-stage strategy or an actual question, and she was not yet sure which.

\"Mr. Serrano,\" she said. \"If you intend to contest the codicil, you should retain counsel today. If you intend to contest the disposition of any specific item, you should retain counsel today. If you intend, in any respect, to take a position adverse to your sister or to Ms. Maldonado in the next two weeks, you should retain counsel today, and I will recommend three names. If you do not intend any of those things — if you intend, instead, to participate in the appraisal, to listen to the result, to consider in good faith whether to exercise your right of first refusal or to allow another beneficiary to exercise hers, and to settle this estate without litigation — then you do not need your own lawyer. You need a tax advisor, possibly, depending on which way the disposition goes, and I can recommend one. But you do not need counsel adverse to the estate. What you need to decide is which of those two persons you are going to be.\"

He looked at her.

\"I don't know yet,\" he said.

\"That is an honest answer.\"

\"Is it the wrong one.\"

\"It is the only one,\" she said, \"that I will accept from you today. Tell me by Friday.\"

\"All right.\"

\"Mr. Serrano.\"

\"Yes.\"

\"Whichever you decide, decide it because it is what you want and not because it is what you think I want.\"

\"All right.\"

She nodded once. She turned. She walked out of the dining room and down the hall and she let herself out the front door and she went down the stoop into the February morning and she walked two blocks before she allowed herself to take a full breath.

In the office that afternoon she had three other matters to attend to and she attended to them with the efficient and slightly elevated concentration of a person trying to prove to herself that she was still a working attorney with a practice and not the housemother of a single dramatic estate. She returned calls. She reviewed a settlement statement in an unrelated matter. She had a forty-minute meeting with a new client whose father had died intestate in Bucks County and whose family situation, by the standards of the morning Asha had just had, was so straightforward as to be almost relaxing. At four-thirty she got a call from Beverly Ostrowski confirming the inspection for Thursday at ten. At five-fifteen she got an email from Daniel.

The email was three lines long.

\"Counselor — I have thought about your question. I will not be retaining separate counsel. I will see you Thursday. Thank you for yesterday and today. — D. Serrano.\"

She read it twice. She did not reply immediately. She closed the email and opened it again half an hour later and read it a third time. The thank-you at the end was the line she kept returning to. It was placed where in another man's email it would have been placed without thought, as a closing formula, and where in this man's email she suspected it had been placed and then cut and then replaced, possibly more than once, and that the version she was reading was the version he had decided, after some deliberation, he could stand to have written.

She replied at six.

\"Mr. Serrano — Received. I will see you Thursday at the inspection. — A. Mensah.\"

She did not include a thank-you. She wanted, very precisely, to receive his without redeeming him for it. He could keep the thank-you, on his side of the ledger, where it belonged.

At seven she left the office. She walked the long way home, west across Market and then north up Twenty-first, and she stopped at the little place on Pine for soup, and she ate the soup alone at a small table with her phone face-down beside the bowl, and she thought, with the careful and somewhat melancholy attention she gave to such thoughts when she gave them attention at all, about the difference between being moved and being compromised, and about whether Mr. Halloran was right that they were not the same thing, and about the fact that the line between them was not a line, exactly, but a kind of weather, and that the weather over the Serrano estate, at the moment, was changing faster than she could quite keep pace with.

She finished the soup. She paid. She walked home.

Tuesday she did not go to the house. Wednesday she did not go to the house. Wednesday afternoon Lucia called the office, not Asha's cell, which Asha noted with approval, and asked through Marcus whether it would be appropriate for her to send Asha a photograph of an object in the upstairs hall closet whose provenance she could not establish and whose presence in the inventory she wanted to flag, and Asha replied through Marcus that a photograph and a one-paragraph description would be sufficient, and that the inventory would handle it. Wednesday evening Rosa called the office, also not Asha's cell, and asked Marcus whether the appraiser would need access to the third floor or only the first two, and Marcus told her all three and the cellar, and Rosa thanked him and asked, almost as an afterthought, whether the counselor would be present at the inspection, and Marcus said yes, and Rosa said good, and hung up.

Thursday at ten Asha was on the stoop. Beverly Ostrowski arrived two minutes later with a clipboard and a measuring laser and the slightly distracted manner of a person whose entire professional life consisted of looking at other people's homes and assigning numbers to them. Daniel arrived three minutes after that. Lucia opened the door. Rosa was already in the kitchen. The inspection began.

It took four hours.

title: === SCENE 10 ===
content:
=== SCENE 10 ===
Beverly Ostrowski moved through the house room by room, top to bottom, then bottom to top, then a second pass through the principal rooms with the laser. She made notes. She asked questions. She asked about the age of the boiler, the date of the most recent roof work, the condition of the rear addition. Rosa answered the practical questions. Daniel answered the financial questions. Lucia answered the sentimental questions, which were not technically part of the appraisal but which Beverly asked anyway, because Beverly was the kind of appraiser who understood that a row house in Philadelphia was both a financial asset and a fact about a family, and that the family's account of it could not change the number but could change the appraiser's confidence in the number.

At two o'clock Beverly closed her clipboard and said she would have a preliminary number by Friday afternoon and a written report by the following Wednesday, and she shook hands with each of them and let herself out.

In the dining room the four of them sat again.

Asha had brought no folder this time. She had brought only a single sheet of paper, which was the page from the memorandum that listed the options for the meeting two weeks from today, and she laid it on the table without comment.

\"We don't have to talk about this now,\" she said. \"We have until next Wednesday. But the report will not say anything about you. It will say only what the building is worth. The conversation about what to do with the building is the conversation you three are going to have, with or without me in the room, between Wednesday and the meeting the following Monday. I would like to suggest that you have at least the first part of that conversation now, while I am here, because I have noticed in other estates that the conversations that begin in front of a lawyer tend to be slightly more careful than the conversations that begin without one, and that the careful version, once established, tends to persist.\"

She looked at the three of them.

\"Mr. Serrano,\" she said. \"Would you start.\"

He did not look surprised to be asked. He looked, rather, like a man who had been waiting to be asked and who had been rehearsing what he would say and who, now that the moment had come, was discovering that the rehearsal had not survived the morning.

\"I have been thinking,\" he said.

He stopped. He started again.

\"I have been thinking,\" he said, \"about what I said on Monday. About my mother. About — I said she would have hated this. I said it as if I knew what she would have hated. I have been thinking about that since Monday and I do not think I know what she would have hated. I think I know what I would have hated, on her behalf, and I think I have been confusing the two things for a long time, and I think Lucia has known I was confusing the two things for a long time, and I think Rosa has known it longer than either of us, and I — \"

He stopped again.

He looked at Rosa.

\"I owe you an apology,\" he said, \"that is larger than I can make this morning. I am not going to try to make it this morning. I am going to try to make it over time. I want you to know that I know I owe it. That is all I am prepared to say today.\"

Rosa looked at him for a long moment.

\"All right,\" she said.

\"All right,\" Daniel said.

\"Daniel,\" Rosa said.

\"Yes.\"

\"I do not need the apology to be large. I need it to be true. A small true apology is better than a large performed one. You understand.\"

\"I understand.\"

\"All right then.\"

She turned to Asha.

\"Counselor,\" she said. \"May I say something.\"

\"Please.\"

\"I have been thinking, also,\" Rosa said. \"Since Monday. I have been thinking about what your mother\" — she looked at Daniel, then at Lucia — \"what your mother wanted. The codicil says one third, one third, one third. The letter says she wanted us to be kind. These are two different documents. They do not say the same thing. The codicil is the law. The letter is the wish. I have been a housekeeper for thirty-one years and I have a great deal of respect for the difference between the law and the wish. The law is what protects you. The wish is what asks something of you. They are not enemies. But they are not the same.\"

She paused.

\"I do not want the house,\" she said.

Lucia drew in a breath. Daniel did not move.

\"I want you to listen to me,\" Rosa said, \"before you decide what I mean. I do not want the house in the sense that I cannot afford the house and I do not wish to spend my old age in a transaction with the two of you that I would not survive emotionally. I do not want the house in the sense of taking it from you. I am not capable of that and I would not become capable of it. But I do not want to leave the house either. I have lived in the third-floor room since 1996. I would like to continue to live in the third-floor room. I would like to continue to cook in this kitchen, not for wages, because I will not be a housekeeper here any longer, but because I do not know how to be in a kitchen and not cook in it. I would like, if it is possible — and I am asking, I am not telling — I would like for one of you to keep the house. I do not care which one. I would like, in whatever arrangement you make between you, for there to be a room in it for me, named in the document, with a key that is mine and not loaned to me, for as long as I want it. In exchange for that, I will assign my third to whichever of you keeps the house, for one dollar. I have spoken to no lawyer. I am speaking now. I will speak again if you tell me I am wrong to speak.\"

There was a silence.

It was, Asha thought, the largest silence she had heard in this house, and the largest silence she had heard in any house in many years. It had a quality of attention in it that was almost physical, as if the silence itself were leaning forward to listen.

Lucia spoke first.

\"Rosa.\"

\"Yes.\"

\"You cannot do that.\"

\"I am doing it.\"

\"Rosa.\"

\"Lucia. Listen to me. I am sixty-eight years old. I have a sister in Camden and three nieces and a savings account that is larger than your brother thinks it is and smaller than your sister thinks it is. I do not need a building. I need a room. The building is too much for me. The building was too much for your mother and she would not say so. I am saying so. I am saying so because she asked me, in February, to make sure the two of you did not destroy each other over this house, and the way to make sure of that is for the house to belong to one of you and not to be divided into three pieces of which one piece is mine. The codicil was for the law. This conversation is for the wish. Do you understand.\"

\"I understand,\" Lucia said, \"and I do not accept.\"

\"You do not have to accept today.\"

\"I will not accept.\"

\"Lucia.\"

\"Rosa, I will not — \"

\"Lucia,\" Daniel said.

She turned to him, startled.

\"Lucia,\" Daniel said. He was looking at Rosa, not at his sister. \"Let her finish. We can disagree with her in a minute. Let her finish what she is saying first.\"

Lucia closed her mouth.

Rosa looked at Daniel for a long moment.

\"Thank you,\" she said.

\"You're welcome.\"

\"I am finished,\" Rosa said. \"That was what I had to say. Now you can tell me I am wrong.\"

Asha sat very still.

She was, she realized, watching something she had not planned for and could not, in any formal sense, manage. Rosa had taken the conversation out of the legal frame and placed it inside the family frame, and the family frame did not have rules of procedure, and Asha did not run it. She was, for the first time since she had walked into this house on Monday morning, not the central figure in the room. She was a witness.

She did the only thing that seemed to her, in the moment, to be both professionally appropriate and humanly accurate. She picked up her pen, and she set it down, deliberately, on top of the single sheet of paper she had brought with her. She folded her hands. She waited.

Lucia spoke first, finally, in a voice that was much smaller than the voice in which she had said she would not accept.

\"Rosa,\" she said. \"What if I cannot afford the house either.\"

\"Then your brother will keep it,\" Rosa said, \"and you and I will visit. Or your brother will not keep it and we will all leave. The house is not the point. The room is not the point. The point is that your mother wanted you to choose. The codicil made it possible for you to choose. I am trying to make it possible for you to choose without being crushed by money. That is all I am trying to do.\"

\"Daniel,\" Lucia said.

\"Yes.\"

\"Do you want the house.\"

He was quiet for a long time.

\"I wanted to sell the house,\" he said finally, \"and I told myself that was the same as wanting it. I think I do not know yet what I want. I think — I think I want to find out, between now and Monday week, what I want. I am asking you to let me find that out without deciding for me. I am also asking you to find out, between now and Monday week, what you want. I do not want you to tell me today. I want you to tell me when you know.\"

Lucia looked at him.

\"All right,\" she said.

\"All right.\"

He turned to Rosa.

\"Rosa,\" he said. \"I am not accepting your offer today either. I am not refusing it. I am thanking you for it, and I am telling you that the answer it deserves is not an answer I am able to give you this afternoon. I am asking you for the same week I am asking my sister for. Can you give it to me.\"

\"I can give it to you,\" Rosa said.

\"Thank you.\"

He looked, finally, at Asha.

\"Counselor,\" he said. \"Have we conducted ourselves properly.\"

The question was not, she understood, the question he was asking. The question he was asking was whether he had conducted himself properly. The question he had asked aloud was the one he could bear to ask.

\"You have conducted yourselves,\" she said, \"better than I had any right to expect on a Thursday afternoon. We will meet again Monday week. In the meantime, I will be available by telephone at the office, and Marcus will be available by telephone at the office, and the three of you will, I hope, be available to each other.\"

\"Yes,\" Daniel said.

\"Yes,\" Lucia said.

\"Yes,\" Rosa said.

Asha stood.

title: === SCENE 11 ===
content:
=== SCENE 11 ===
She gathered the single sheet of paper. She put it back in her bag. She put on her coat in the hall this time without Lucia's help, and she said her goodbyes at the front door without crossing the threshold of the dining room again, and she went down the stoop into a Thursday afternoon that had turned, while she was inside, into a thin and surprising sunlight, and she stood for a moment at the bottom of the steps with her hand on the iron railing.

She did not yet know, she realized, what would happen in that house between now and Monday week. She did not know whether Daniel would, in the privacy of the days ahead, find the version of himself he had glimpsed at the table or lose it again. She did not know whether Lucia would accept Rosa's offer or refuse it on principle and then refuse it again on a different principle until the offer became a wound between them. She did not know whether Rosa, having said the largest thing she had said in thirty-one years, would be able to say anything else for a while, or whether the saying of it had opened in her a door she had kept closed for very good reasons and could not now easily close again.

She did not know any of these things. She knew only that the codicil had been filed, and that the buyers were gone, and that the appraisal would arrive on Wednesday, and that on Monday week the three of them would sit in that dining room again and decide, in front of her or without her, what the rest of their lives in relation to this building and to each other was going to look like, and that whatever they decided would, by the operation of the documents she had drafted and the conversations she had presided over and the small careful refusals she had made of lunches and first names and evening telephone calls, be a decision they had made and not a decision that had been made for them.

She let go of the railing.

She walked to the corner. At the corner she stopped and turned and looked back at the house. From this angle, in the afternoon light, the brick was the color it must have been when it was new, and the cornice line was clean against the pale sky, and a single curtain in the second-floor window — the sewing-room window, she realized — moved very slightly, as if someone inside had touched it in passing and not meant to.

She turned the corner and walked east, toward the office, and toward the week that was about to begin.","title":"Part 3"}

The week that began on Friday morning began for Asha with the ordinary problem of a docket. She had, besides the Serrano estate, a small contested guardianship in Bucks County, a will whose witnessing she needed to defend by affidavit, two intake calls she had postponed twice, and a partner's meeting at four. She arrived at the office at seven-forty, which was earlier than she usually arrived and earlier than she had told herself she would arrive, and she made coffee in the small kitchen and stood at the window of her office looking at the brick of the building opposite, which was not the brick of the Serrano house but resembled it in the way that all old Philadelphia brick resembles all other old Philadelphia brick when the morning light is thin.

She had made, the night before, a list. The list was on a yellow pad on her desk and it had seven items on it, of which the first was "call Marcus re: filing confirmation," the second was "draft consent to extension for buyers (if any return)," the third was "appraisal Wed — confirm appraiser," the fourth was "Monday week meeting — agenda?," the fifth was "Rosa — separate consultation? conflict?," the sixth was "Lucia — letter," and the seventh, written in smaller handwriting and underlined twice, was the single word "neutrality."

She looked at the seventh item for some time and then she crossed it out, not because she had resolved it but because seeing it written down made it harder, somehow, to do the thing it was meant to remind her to do. She wrote in its place, in the same small handwriting, "remember why you do this work."

Then she called Marcus.

Marcus had filed the codicil on Thursday evening at four-fifteen, twenty minutes before the Register of Wills closed. He had filed it under cover of an explanatory letter that Asha had drafted in the car on the way back from the house, and he had paid the filing fee out of the retainer, and he had brought back a stamped copy which was now in the file on her desk and a digital scan which was now in the cloud folder she shared with herself. The codicil existed, in other words, in the world in three places at once, which was as close to permanence as any document achieved in this profession.

"They will contest it," Marcus said, by way of greeting, when he picked up.

"Who will."

"Whoever is going to. The buyers, if they come back and find out the contingency they were depending on is gone. The brother, eventually, if he reverts to type. The IRS, conceivably, if the valuation comes in higher than the basis we are going to claim."

"The brother is not going to contest it."

"You sound certain."

"I am not certain. I am hopeful. There is a difference and I am holding onto it because it is Friday morning and I have not had enough coffee."

"Asha."

"What."

"You are not their friend."

She held the phone away from her ear for a moment and then brought it back.

"I know," she said.

"I am not saying this to reprimand you. I am saying this because I have watched you for three years and I have seen you do this work better than anyone I know and I have also seen the cases where you came close to mistaking the people for the work, and this one has all the markings."

"Which markings."

"The daughter who looks at you a certain way. The housekeeper who has decided to trust you. The son who has, against the odds, started to behave. You like them. You like that they are starting to behave because of something you did. That is the dangerous part. That is the part where lawyers begin to make decisions on behalf of clients instead of for clients."

"I have not made any decisions on their behalf."

"I know you have not. I am saying that the conditions for it exist. I am saying it now while it is still possible to say it."

"Thank you, Marcus."

"Do not thank me. Buy me lunch."

"I will buy you lunch on Friday of next week. After Monday."

"Tuesday."

"Tuesday."

She hung up and sat for some time with her hand on the receiver, and then she picked up the yellow pad and wrote, beneath the items already there, an eighth item: "Marcus — Tuesday lunch — listen."

The day went the way days went. The guardianship matter required two telephone calls and a memo. The affidavit took an hour. The intake calls were both, as intake calls tended to be, longer and stranger than they had appeared on her schedule, one of them a man whose father had died intestate in 2019 and whose siblings had decided five years later that this was finally the moment to discuss it, the other a woman who wanted to know whether she could disinherit a son who had not spoken to her in eleven years and whose name she could not, during the call, bring herself to say aloud. Asha listened to both of them with the part of her attention that was trained to listen and made notes with the part of her that was trained to make notes and underneath these two activities the other part of her, the part she did not have a name for, was thinking about the second-floor window and the curtain that had moved.

At two in the afternoon her assistant put through a call from Lucia.

"I am sorry to call you at work," Lucia said.

"It is what the office line is for. Are you all right."

"I am all right. I am calling because Daniel came over this morning and we had breakfast together for the first time in I cannot remember how long, and I wanted to tell you that, and I did not want to tell you that on your cell because I remembered you said the office line was for office things, and this is, I suppose, an office thing, because it concerns the estate, although it does not concern any particular item of the estate."

"I am glad you called the office line."

"He brought bagels."

"That is a Daniel thing to do."

"It is. He brought bagels and lox and cream cheese and capers and the small red onion sliced very thin, which is the way our mother used to slice it, and he set the table in the kitchen, not the dining room, and we ate breakfast and we did not talk about the house for the first forty minutes and then we talked about the house for two hours and now he is gone and I am sitting in the kitchen looking at the plates and I wanted to tell someone, and the someone I wanted to tell was you, and I am aware of what that means and I am telling you anyway because you said to be honest with you and I am being honest with you."

Asha closed her eyes for a moment and opened them.

"Lucia," she said.

"I know."

"I am glad you and your brother had breakfast. I am glad you talked. I cannot be the person you tell about it. Not yet. Not while I am the lawyer on this estate. After. If you want to, after."

There was a silence on the line that was not, Asha could tell, an angry silence. It was the silence of a person absorbing something she had half-expected.

"All right," Lucia said.

"I am sorry."

"Do not be sorry. I would have been disappointed if you had said anything else. I would have called you anyway, but I would have been disappointed."

"Was there anything about the estate, specifically, that you needed to tell me."

"Yes. He asked me whether I would consider, if he bought out my share of the house at fair market value, staying in it for a year while he decided what he wanted to do with it. He said he was not asking me to decide today. He said he was telling me he was considering asking me, and he wanted to know whether the question was one I would be willing to receive in two weeks."

"What did you tell him."

"I told him I would be willing to receive the question. I told him I had not yet decided what I wanted either, and that I would not pretend to have decided in order to give him an answer, and that if he asked me in two weeks I would tell him what I knew then and not before."

"That was well said."

"It was your phrasing. I borrowed it."

"You are welcome to it."

"Asha."

"Yes."

"Is it improper of me to tell you that I am — that I am grateful to you. In an estate sense. As a client. Is that a thing a client is permitted to say."

"That is a thing a client is permitted to say. Thank you."

"Good. Then I am saying it. In an estate sense."

"In an estate sense, received and noted."

title: === SCENE 12 ===
content:
=== SCENE 12 ===
"I will see you Monday week."

"Monday week."

She hung up and put both hands flat on her desk and breathed in and out four times, which was a thing she had taught herself to do in law school during the trial advocacy class and which she had not had to do, in a professional context, for some time.

The afternoon went on. She drafted an agenda for the Monday week meeting, which was a short document with five items, of which the first was "review of filed codicil and its operative effect," the second was "review of appraisal," the third was "discussion of options re: disposition of the residence," the fourth was "discussion of timeline and any extensions required," and the fifth was "next steps." She emailed the agenda to Marcus and to no one else, because the practice she preferred was to bring the agenda to the meeting in printed form and distribute it there, so that the document had the weight of an artifact rather than the lightness of an email. She would, over the weekend, refine it.

At four she went to the partner's meeting, which concerned an entirely different set of matters and which lasted forty minutes and which she contributed to competently and without distinction. At five-fifteen she came back to her office and stood at her desk and decided that she would not stay late on a Friday and she would not work over the weekend on the Serrano matter except to think about it, which was a form of work she could not avoid and would not try to.

She went home. She lived in a small apartment on Pine Street that she had rented seven years ago intending to stay one year, and which she had stayed in because she had never gotten around to looking for somewhere better and because the light in the front room in the late afternoon was a light she had become attached to in a way she had not become attached to many things. She made dinner. She read for an hour. She slept badly and woke at four and lay for some time looking at the ceiling and thinking not about the codicil but about the curtain.

The curtain had moved.

She had decided, on Thursday evening, that it had moved because Lucia, or possibly Rosa, had walked past the window inside the sewing room, and that the movement of air a person creates by walking past a curtained window is enough to stir the curtain, and that this was a perfectly ordinary mechanical fact about curtains and the bodies of people and the rooms of old houses, and that her noticing it as she had noticed it, with a feeling of being seen, was the kind of perceptual error a tired professional makes at the end of a hard week, and that the appropriate response to such an error was to file it and forget it.

She had filed it. She had not forgotten it.

She got up at five-thirty and made coffee.

—

On Saturday morning, Rosa walked from her apartment on Catharine Street to the Italian Market and bought what she had bought every Saturday for thirty-one years, which was a half-pound of provolone, a loaf of bread from the bakery on Christian Street, and a small bag of the small dark olives that Mrs. Serrano had liked and that Rosa had continued to buy for herself after Mrs. Serrano stopped being able to chew them. She brought these things home and put them in her own refrigerator, which was a thing she had not done very often before, because she had been in the habit, for thirty-one years, of bringing them to the house on Spruce Street.

She made herself breakfast. She ate it standing at the counter, which was a habit she had developed in a kitchen she had cleaned for other people and which had become so much a part of her body that she could not, even in her own kitchen, sit down to a meal she had prepared for herself alone.

The telephone rang at ten.

It was Daniel.

"Rosa," he said. "I am calling to ask you something and I want to be clear that I am not asking it through the lawyer and I am not asking it as the executor and I am asking it as myself."

"All right, Daniel."

"I would like to come and have coffee with you. Not at the house. At wherever you would prefer. I would like to apologize to you, in a sentence or two, for some specific things, and I would like to ask you, after that, a question about my mother that I do not feel I can ask my sister and that I cannot ask anyone else who is still alive."

Rosa held the phone for a moment. She had spent thirty-one years anticipating, among other things, the conversations Daniel might one day have the courage to ask her for, and she had imagined this one specifically, and the imagining of it had made her cautious. She had imagined that when it came, if it came, she would say no, because she had decided long ago that she did not owe him the conversation and that giving it to him would cost her more than she could afford to spend.

"Yes," she heard herself say. "There is a place on Tenth Street. The bakery with the green awning. They have tables in the back. I can be there at three."

"Three. Thank you, Rosa. Thank you."

"Daniel."

"Yes."

"I am not promising you the answer to the question. I am promising you the coffee and the apology. The question I will decide about when I hear it."

"Understood."

She hung up and stood for some time with her hand on the receiver, which was, she realized, the same gesture Asha had made the day before in an office Rosa had never seen. The gestures of people who have just said something they did not know they were going to say are, perhaps, more similar than the people themselves are.

She put on her coat at two-thirty and walked to Tenth Street.

The bakery had a green awning and four small tables in the back room and a glass case in front that held the cannoli Rosa had not bought in a long time because she had stopped, for reasons she did not examine, buying things for herself that she had bought for Mrs. Serrano. She ordered a coffee and a plain biscotto and sat at the table farthest from the door, which gave her a view of who came in.

Daniel came in at three exactly.

He was wearing a sweater she had not seen before, which was a softer sweater than the sweaters he ordinarily wore, and he had not shaved, which she had also not seen before, and he stood at the counter and ordered his coffee in passable Italian, which she had also not heard from him before, although she had known he had taken Italian in college and had not, in twenty-two years, used it in her presence. He brought his coffee back to the table and sat down across from her and put his hands flat on the table the way people do when they have rehearsed a thing they are about to say.

"Rosa," he said. "I want to apologize for three specific things, in order of how long ago they happened. The first is that when I was sixteen I told you, in the kitchen, that you were not part of the family. I have remembered saying that for twenty-six years and I have never apologized for it and I am apologizing for it now. The second is that when my mother was sick, in the last six months, I assumed that you were being paid enough to do what you were doing and I did not, on any of my visits, thank you for what you were doing or ask whether you needed help doing it. I am apologizing for that. The third is that on Thursday, in the dining room, before I read the document, I spoke about you as if you were not in the room. I am apologizing for that."

Rosa looked at him.

"Daniel," she said. "I accept the apologies. The first one in particular I have been waiting for, and I am glad to have it, and I will not pretend I am not. The second one is more complicated and we can talk about it if you want. The third one I had already, in my head, forgiven, because I watched you forgive yourself for it later in the same afternoon, and watching that was, in its way, enough."

He swallowed.

"Thank you," he said.

"What is the question."

He looked down at his coffee. He looked up.

"Did she know," he said. "Did she know that I was — that I was the way I was. With her. In the last years. Did she know that I was performing being a good son rather than being one. Did she see through it. Did she — was the codicil — was it because she saw through it. I need to know whether she saw through it. I have been thinking about this since Wednesday and I cannot work out whether the worst thing is that she saw through it or the worst thing is that she did not see through it and made the codicil anyway because she had simply, on the merits and without reference to my failures, decided that you and Lucia deserved the house more than I did. I do not know which would be worse. I need someone who was there to tell me what she saw."

Rosa took a breath.

She had imagined this question. She had imagined it for years. She had imagined answering it in several different ways depending on the man Daniel had become by the time he asked it, and she had imagined that the worst version of the answer would be the version she gave to the worst version of him, and the best version of the answer would be the version she gave to the best version of him, and she had imagined, also, that the man asking the question might have become a different man by the asking of it, and that the answer might therefore have to be adjusted in the moment.

She looked at him across the table. He had not shaved. He had ordered his coffee in Italian. He had apologized for three specific things in chronological order, which was the way a man apologizes who has been making a list.

"She saw through it," Rosa said. "And it did not matter."

He flinched.

title: === SCENE 13 ===
content:
=== SCENE 13 ===
"I will say it again," Rosa said, "because I want you to hear it the second time. She saw through it. And it did not matter. She loved you, Daniel. She loved you the way she loved you, which was not the way you wanted to be loved, and she knew it was not the way you wanted to be loved, and she could not change the way she loved you any more than you could change the way you wanted to be loved, and she made her peace with that long before she got sick. The codicil was not a punishment. It was not even a correction. It was, as far as I could tell from the conversations I had with her in the kitchen on the afternoons when she was telling me what she was thinking — and she did tell me, Daniel, she told me because there was no one else in the house to tell — it was a recognition. She recognized that the house had become a place she lived in with me and that Lucia visited often, and she recognized that you had built a life elsewhere, and she recognized that leaving the house to you would force you to either sell it, which would cost you something, or keep it, which would cost you more, and she decided that what she wanted to leave you was the freedom from that decision. She thought she was being kind to you."

He was crying.

He was crying without sound, which was a way of crying Rosa had seen him do once before, when he was eleven and had failed to make a team he had wanted to make, and which she had not seen him do since.

"She was wrong," he said, after a while. "She was wrong about what would be kind."

"She was wrong," Rosa said. "She was often wrong about you. She was wrong about you in the direction of thinking better of you than you thought of yourself, which is a direction mothers are often wrong in, and which it is the work of sons to either grow into or never recover from. I do not know yet which you are going to do. I am hopeful."

He laughed, once, a wet startled laugh.

"Rosa."

"Yes."

"I do not want to sell the house."

"I know."

"I do not know what I want to do with it. But I do not want to sell it. I have known I did not want to sell it since Wednesday afternoon when I sat in the dining room and I could not get the words out of my mouth, and I have been trying since then to find a story I could tell myself in which I had to sell it anyway because of the debts and the taxes and the practicality, and I have not been able to find one that holds together for more than an hour at a time, and I am tired of looking for one."

"Then stop looking for one."

"There are still the debts."

"There are always debts. The house has been there for a hundred and forty years and it has outlasted every debt anyone in it ever had. It will outlast yours. There are ways. There are second mortgages, and there are equity arrangements, and there are renters in the third-floor apartment, and there are siblings who might, if asked properly, agree to a structure that lets the house stay a house. You have a lawyer. Ask her."

"I cannot ask her certain things."

"You can ask her about the structures. The other things you will work out yourself, or you will not, and the house will stand regardless. The house does not require you to work out the other things. The house requires only that you not sell it to someone who will tear out the kitchen."

He laughed again. He wiped his face with the back of his hand, which was a gesture she had also seen him do at eleven.

"Rosa," he said. "About the room. About what was in the document. About your room."

"Yes."

"I would like, if you are willing, to draw up a separate agreement, outside the estate, between you and me personally, that gives you that room for the rest of your life regardless of what happens to the house. I would like to do this even if we keep the house. I would like to do it because my mother intended it and because the document only operates if we keep the house and I do not yet know whether we will keep the house and I do not want your security to depend on a question that has not been answered. Would you let me do that."

Rosa looked at him for a long time.

"I would let you do that," she said. "On one condition."

"Name it."

"That you do it through your sister's lawyer. I do not mean Asha. I mean a different lawyer, one your sister approves of, so that the agreement is not a thing you and I have done between us in secret and so that Lucia knows from the start that it exists and what it says. I have spent thirty-one years being a secret between members of this family in one way or another. I am too old to start a new secret today."

"Agreed."

"And Daniel."

"Yes."

"Thank you. For the offer. I want you to know I am thanking you for it before I tell you the other thing, which is that I do not know yet whether I want the room. I have lived in my own apartment on Catharine Street for thirty-one years and I have a life there I have made by myself and that no one in your family has ever seen, and the offer to come and live in the room I cleaned for thirty-one years is an offer I want to think about, because the answer to it is not as obvious as it might appear to you. So I am asking you for what you asked your sister for. I am asking you for the week."

"You can have the week."

"Thank you."

They drank their coffee. They did not say anything else for some time. At ten to four Daniel stood and put on his coat and looked down at her.

"Rosa," he said. "If I had been a different kind of man for the last twenty years."

"You were not a different kind of man for the last twenty years. You were the kind of man you were. You are becoming, possibly, a different kind of man now. That is the thing in front of you. The other thing is not."

"Yes."

"Go home, Daniel. Or go to your sister. Or go for a walk. Do not go back to the house tonight. Give her the evening."

"All right."

He left.

Rosa sat at the table for another twenty minutes. She finished her coffee and she ate the biscotto and she watched the door of the bakery open and close several times for several different customers, and she thought, with a clarity she had not expected, that she had just done a thing she had been preparing to do for thirty-one years and that she did not know what she was going to do with the rest of the time she had been preparing.

She walked home along Tenth Street and turned east on Pine and went the long way past the small park where a dog she did not know was chasing a tennis ball that a child she did not know was throwing, and she stopped for a moment to watch them, and the child threw the ball badly and the dog caught it anyway, and Rosa was surprised to find that she was, herself, almost crying, which was a thing she did not, as a rule, allow herself to do in public.

She went home. She made dinner. She ate it sitting at the table, which she had not done in some years.

—

On Sunday Lucia took the train to her brother's apartment in Fitler Square, which she had been to only twice in eight years, and they spent the afternoon together. What they said to each other Asha would not know and did not need to know. They came back to the house on Spruce Street separately, Daniel returning to his own apartment in the evening and Lucia returning to the house alone, and Lucia sat that night in the sewing room with the light off and the curtain not quite closed and watched the street the way her mother had used to watch the street, and decided, in the watching, several things she had not been able to decide before.

On Monday morning the appraiser came. He was a man in his sixties named Pelletier who had appraised houses in this neighborhood for thirty years and who carried a clipboard and a laser measure and very few opinions, which was, in Asha's experience, what one wanted in an appraiser. He spent three hours in the house. He measured the rooms and photographed the moldings and tapped the plaster and went down into the basement with Lucia and up onto the roof with no one and came down again with his hair slightly disordered and his clipboard full. He told Lucia, at the door, that he would have the report by Wednesday morning, and that the number would not be the number the buyers had offered, and that it would not be the number any sane seller would refuse if a sane buyer made it, but that those two numbers were not, in his experience, the same number, and that the question of what to do with the difference was not his question to answer.

Lucia thanked him.

She called Asha from the kitchen after he left.

"He says it will be by Wednesday morning."

"Good."

"Asha."

"Yes."

"My brother and I are not going to sell the house."

Asha set down her pen.

"Tell me," she said.

"We do not know yet what we are going to do. We have agreed that we are not going to sell. We have agreed that the things we are going to do instead will require structures, and that the structures will require you, and that we will come on Monday week prepared to discuss the structures rather than the question of whether to sell. We have agreed that Rosa is part of the conversation about the structures, not as an employee and not as a witness but as a person whose presence in the house is, in our shared view, not negotiable. We have agreed that we will not pretend, in your presence or in any other professional setting, that we have agreed about more than we have agreed about, and that we will bring our remaining disagreements to the table on Monday week rather than try to resolve them privately first. Is this — is this the kind of thing it is permissible to tell you on the office line."

"This is exactly the kind of thing it is permissible to tell me on the office line."

"Good."

"Lucia."

"Yes."

"Thank you for telling me."

"Thank you for being someone we wanted to tell."

Asha hung up.

She sat at her desk for a long time. She picked up the agenda she had drafted on Friday and she crossed out the third item, which had read "discussion of options re: disposition of the residence," and she wrote in its place, "discussion of structures for retention of the residence." She crossed out the fourth item, which had read "discussion of timeline and any extensions required," and wrote in its place, "discussion of timeline and financing." She left the fifth item as it was.

Then she called Marcus.

"They are keeping the house," she said.

title: === SCENE 14 ===
content:
=== SCENE 14 ===
"Of course they are."

"You knew."

"I suspected. The brother who refuses to read his own ultimatum is not a brother who is going to sell. The sister who hid the letter is not a sister who is going to let him. The housekeeper who waited thirty-one years to speak was not waiting in order to watch the house go to strangers. The only person in the room on Thursday who did not know they were keeping the house was you, and that was because you were the only person in the room whose job required not knowing it until they told you."

"I see."

"Do not be embarrassed. It is your job not to assume. It is my job to assume. That is why there are two of us."

"Thank you, Marcus."

"Tuesday lunch is still on."

"Tuesday lunch is still on."

She hung up and looked at the agenda and thought about what structures were available to a brother and a sister and a non-relative who wished to retain a house in probate against the pressure of debts that would not retreat just because the house was being kept. There were several. There was a buyout of one sibling's interest by the other, financed by a mortgage. There was a partition agreement that allocated use without forcing sale. There was a life estate carved out for Rosa, formalizing what the codicil had already informally accomplished. There was a small-business arrangement under which the third-floor apartment, which she had noticed on her first visit had a separate entrance off the side alley, could be rented out to generate income. There were combinations of these. There were complications. There were tax consequences. There was, in short, work to do, the kind of work she liked doing, the kind of work that bent the hard fact of money into shapes that allowed the soft fact of human attachment to survive a little longer than money ordinarily allowed.

She began to make notes.

—

On Tuesday she had lunch with Marcus at the place on Sansom Street that they had been having lunch at for three years, and she listened to him more than she talked, which was what she had promised herself she would do, and what he said to her was mostly about other cases and about a partner who was retiring and about his daughter's college applications, and only at the end, over coffee, did he say, "You held the line."

"I held the line."

"You did not have lunch with her."

"I did not have lunch with her."

"You will, after."

"I do not know yet."

"You should."

She looked at him.

"You should," he said again. "After. When the estate is closed and the structures are signed and there is no longer any professional reason for you not to. You should have lunch with her. You are allowed. The rule exists for the duration of the representation. The rule does not exist for the rest of your life."

"Marcus."

"I am not telling you what to do. I am telling you what the rule says and what it does not say. The other part is your business."

"Thank you."

"Do not thank me. Pay for lunch."

She paid for lunch.

—

On Wednesday morning the appraisal arrived. The number was, as Pelletier had said it would be, both higher than the buyers had offered and lower than any sane seller would refuse, and Asha sent it to all three clients by email at nine-fifteen, and by ten she had received three acknowledgments, all of which were polite and brief and none of which contained any expression of surprise or distress, which was, she thought, the closest thing to a triumph her profession permitted itself.

The rest of the week passed in drafting. She drafted three possible structures and circulated all three with a covering memo that did not recommend among them. She drafted, separately and at Daniel's specific request, a side agreement between Daniel and Rosa concerning the life occupancy of the second-floor bedroom and bathroom, to be reviewed by independent counsel for Rosa before execution, and she put Marcus in touch with a lawyer at another firm whom Rosa would meet on Friday afternoon at four. She drafted a partition-in-use agreement between Daniel and Lucia. She drafted the outlines of a refinancing memorandum that would, if Daniel chose to go that route, allow him to buy out a portion of Lucia's interest at a price both could accept. She did not draft an opinion as to which structure was best. That was not her job.

On Friday evening she went home and made herself dinner and sat at the small table by the window in her front room and ate it and looked out at Pine Street in the early dark, and she thought about the curtain in the second-floor window, and she thought about the fact that on Monday she would walk back into the dining room of the Serrano house for what might or might not be the last formal meeting of the estate, and that the people on the other side of the table from her had, in the eight days since she had last seen them, done more work on themselves than she had imagined any of them capable of, and that this work was theirs and not hers but that she had been, in some way she did not yet know how to think about, present at the doing of it.

She washed the dish.

She slept.

—

Saturday morning Asha woke early and did not work. She walked in the morning to the river and along it for an hour and back, and she stopped at the market and bought bread and cheese and fruit for the weekend, and she thought, walking back along Pine Street with the paper bag against her hip, about her own father, who had been dead for nine years and whose small estate she had administered herself, and about the conversations she had not had with him before he died and the conversations she had not had with her brother after, and about the way the work she did for other people was also, in a manner she was not always willing to examine, the work she had not been able to do for herself.

She thought about the woman whose intake call she had taken on Friday afternoon, the second one, who had not been able to say her son's name. She thought about Lucia's letter, which she had not read and which she would not read, and which existed now only as a private fact between Lucia and her dead mother, a fact that had done its work by being mentioned aloud in a dining room and need not be examined further by anyone. She thought about Rosa, who had spent thirty-one years being a secret in this family and who had decided last Thursday, in the same dining room, to stop. She thought about Daniel, who had ordered coffee in Italian and apologized for things in chronological order and cried without sound and decided not to sell the house his mother had wanted him not to sell.

She thought about her own boundaries, which she had held, and about her own attachments, which she had not yet decided what to do with, and about the difference between the two, which she understood now to be not a wall but a hinge.

She came home and put the food in the kitchen and sat in the front room and watched the afternoon light move across the floor, which was the light she had stayed in this apartment seven years for, and she thought, for the first time in some weeks, that she was, in spite of everything, doing the work she was meant to do.

On Sunday she drove out to her mother's, which she did once a month, and she sat with her mother on the porch and listened to her mother tell her about the neighbor's dog and the neighbor's grandson and the price of vegetables, and she did not, this time, find herself impatient. She thought, while her mother talked, that her mother also lived in a house, and that someday her mother also would not, and that she had so far not been able to bring herself to think about that day, and that the Serrano estate had made it, very slightly, possible to begin.

She drove home in the dark.

She slept, badly again, and woke at four, and lay looking at the ceiling, and at five she got up and made coffee and sat at the kitchen table with the agenda for Monday in front of her and read it through once and then again, and she crossed out nothing and added nothing, and at six she got dressed.

—

Monday morning was cold and bright. The kind of morning, she thought, that the city offered as a small apology for the kind of week that was about to begin. She walked from her apartment to the office and from the office, at ten-forty, to the house on Spruce Street, and she stood on the stoop for a moment before she rang the bell, because she wanted to mark, to herself, that this was a different arrival from the arrivals before. The codicil had been filed. The buyers were gone. The appraisal was in. The structures had been circulated. The siblings had decided what they had decided. Whatever was going to happen now was going to happen inside a room she had helped to make possible but in which she would not, today, be the most important person.

She rang the bell.

Rosa opened it.

Rosa was wearing a sweater Asha had not seen before, a soft gray one, and her hair was pinned differently, and she was holding a coffee cup, which Asha had also not seen her do, and she stepped back from the door and said, "Come in, Asha. They are in the dining room. I brought pastries this morning, which I did not bring as the housekeeper. I brought them as a person who likes pastries. I want to be clear about that before you eat one."

"I will eat one on those terms," Asha said.

"Good."

She crossed the threshold. The house smelled of coffee and of the pastries Rosa had not brought as the housekeeper and of the faint underlying smell of old wood and old wallpaper and the lavender sachets Mrs. Serrano had kept in the linen closet for forty years and that someone, presumably Lucia, had been replacing as needed. The hallway was warm. Light came down the stairs from the second-floor landing, where a window faced east.

In the dining room Daniel and Lucia were sitting on the same side of the table, which they had not done before. They stood when she came in, which they had also not done before. The table was set for four, with the pastries on a plate in the middle and a fresh pot of coffee and four cups, and there were yellow pads at each place and pens, and at the head of the table, which was the place Asha had not previously sat in, a chair had been pulled out for her.

She set down her bag.

"Good morning," she said.

"Good morning," they said, all three of them, almost in unison, and then laughed, briefly, at the unison.

title: === SCENE 15 ===
content:
=== SCENE 15 ===
"I have brought the agenda," she said, and took it out of her bag, and distributed it around the table, and sat down in the chair that had been pulled out for her, and looked, for one moment before she began, at the three of them across the table from her: at Daniel, who had shaved this morning and whose hands were resting still on the yellow pad in front of him; at Lucia, who was wearing the small gold earrings Asha now recognized as her mother's; at Rosa, who was sitting at the table on the family side and not standing at the sideboard, and who met Asha's eyes and held them, and nodded once.

"All right," Asha said. "Let us begin."

Outside, the sun moved a little further up the brick of the house across the street. Inside, the four of them bent over their yellow pads, and the work of deciding what to do with what was left began.

The agenda Asha had brought was three pages long, single-spaced, and she had numbered every item, which was a habit she did not always indulge but which this particular morning seemed to require, because the things that needed to be decided in this room today had a way of escaping into adjacent rooms if they were not held down by numbers. She read the first item aloud.

"Confirmation of the codicil as the operative testamentary instrument," she said. "I want to walk through this once on the record, in front of all of you, so that if any of you intends to object, you object now, in this room, and not later, in a filing."

Daniel looked at his sister. Lucia looked at her brother. Then they both looked back at Asha, and Daniel said, "I do not intend to object."

"Lucia."

"I do not intend to object."

"Rosa, you are not a beneficiary under the codicil. You are a witness to it. I am not asking you to assent. I am asking whether, to your memory, the document we filed is the document your employer signed in your presence on the date it bears."

"It is," Rosa said.

"Thank you. We will move to item two."

Item two was the appraisal. The house had come in higher than Daniel had hoped and lower than Lucia had feared, which Asha had told them, privately, the week before, was usually a sign that the appraisal was honest. The number sat on the page between them now like a small piece of furniture they had to walk around. Daniel reached for his coffee and did not drink from it. Lucia put her hand flat on the page, briefly, as if the number were warm.

"The codicil," Asha said, "leaves the house to Lucia, with a charge upon the property in favor of Daniel in the amount of one-third of the appraised value, payable on a schedule we will discuss in item four. It also provides a life tenancy in the third-floor rooms to Rosa, terminable only at her election. The residue of the estate, after debts and taxes, divides equally between Daniel and Lucia. That is the instrument. Item three. Debts."

They moved into the debts, which were the part of any estate that no family ever wanted to look at, because debts were the place where the dead had been most alone. Mrs. Serrano had carried a small line of credit on the house, which Asha had paid down during the week from estate funds. She had owed the gas company a sum that had embarrassed Daniel when he learned of it. She had owed her cardiologist's office a final bill that Lucia had asked, quietly, to pay personally, and Asha had told her she could not, because it would complicate the accounting, and Lucia had said all right, and they had moved on. There was a credit card with a balance that Daniel had assumed was much larger than it turned out to be, and when Asha read the actual number aloud he made a small sound that was not quite a laugh.

"She was more careful than I thought," he said.

"She was more careful than any of you thought," Rosa said, and it was the first thing she had said since the confirmation of the codicil, and it landed in the room without any of the edge it might have carried two weeks ago. It was simply a statement of fact, delivered by the person in the room best positioned to know.

"Item four," Asha said. "The schedule of payment on the charge."

This was the item that had taken her the longest to draft, because it was the item in which the family had to decide, in numbers, what kind of family they were going to try to be. Daniel needed money. He had told her that on the second day, in the kitchen, without quite telling her that, and she had understood, and she had not held it against him, because need was not a character flaw, although the things people did because of it sometimes were. Lucia did not have a third of the appraised value in cash. No one in the room expected her to. The question was over how long a period, on what terms, and with what security, the charge would be paid.

Daniel had a proposal. Lucia had a proposal. Asha had a proposal. They had exchanged these over email through the weekend, and the proposals had begun very far apart and ended, by Sunday night, within shouting distance of one another, and the purpose of this morning was to close the remaining distance.

"Daniel," Asha said. "Walk us through where you are."

He did. He spoke for perhaps four minutes. He did not raise his voice. He did not, Asha noticed, use any of the phrases he had used in the first week: not "what I am owed," not "by right," not "before anyone else gets clever." He said he had thought about it over the weekend, and that he understood Lucia could not refinance immediately, and that he was willing to accept a longer amortization than he had originally asked for if the interest rate was indexed in a way he described in some detail, and Asha let him describe it, because describing it was a way of giving him back a piece of the competence he had spent the last two weeks misusing. When he finished, he looked at his sister.

"Lucia."

Lucia spoke for perhaps three minutes. She said that she was willing to accept the higher of the two rates Daniel had proposed if he was willing to accept a longer term. She said she had spoken with her bank in New York and that she could put down a sum at closing larger than the one she had originally offered, because she had decided to sell her apartment, which was a thing she had not told anyone in the room, including Asha, before this moment.

Asha did not let her face change. Daniel's face changed. He looked at his sister and said, "Lucia."

"I have thought about it," she said. "I do not need two homes. I have not, really, lived in New York for some time. I have been editing from hotels and other people's spare rooms for three years. I can edit from here. I would like to edit from here. The apartment is worth what it is worth, and what it is worth is enough to make this easier for both of us."

"You don't have to do that."

"I know I don't have to."

"I'm not asking you to."

"I know you're not. I am telling you what I have decided to do. It is not for you. It is for the arrangement. It is also, partly, for me."

Daniel was quiet. Then he said, "All right."

"All right," Lucia said.

Asha wrote a note on her pad. The note said: *larger down payment at closing, schedule revised accordingly, draft by Wednesday.* She underlined *Wednesday* and then, after a moment, crossed out the underline, because there was no longer any particular urgency about Wednesday. The urgency had gone out of the file at some point over the last forty-eight hours and she had not, until this moment, noticed it leaving.

"Item five," she said. "The life tenancy."

Rosa straightened slightly in her chair. Asha had walked Rosa through the language on Friday, in the office, with the door closed, and Rosa had read it twice and then asked two questions, both of them practical, both of them sharp, and Asha had answered them, and Rosa had said, "All right, then," and signed nothing, because there was nothing yet to sign. Today there was something to sign. Asha had brought it in a folder.

"The life tenancy," Asha said, "gives Rosa the use of the third-floor rooms for as long as she wishes them. It does not require her to live there. It does not require her to pay rent. It does not require her to perform any service in the house. It is not contingent on her employment, which, as of the date of Mrs. Serrano's death, ended. It is a gift, made by your mother, with the consent of both of you in your capacity as residual beneficiaries, and accepted, if she chooses to accept it, by Rosa."

"I choose to accept it," Rosa said.

"I will witness her signature when we reach that point. Before we do, I want each of you to say, on the record, that you understand what the life tenancy is and that you do not contest it."

"I understand," Daniel said. "I do not contest it."

"I understand," Lucia said. "I do not contest it. I am glad of it."

"Rosa, do you have any questions before you sign?"

"I have one."

"Please."

Rosa looked at the two siblings across the table. "If I take this," she said, "I am still your mother's housekeeper in the sense that I knew her better than anyone alive in this room except you two, and possibly better than that. I am not your mother's housekeeper in the sense that I will clean this house. I want to be clear that the life tenancy is not a way of keeping me here as staff. If I am here, I am here as a person who lived with your mother for thirty-one years and who does not, at this point in her life, particularly want to start over somewhere else. Is that the understanding."

"That is the understanding," Lucia said.

"That is the understanding," Daniel said, and then he added, which Asha had not expected him to add, "and I am sorry it took me as long as it did to arrive at it."

Rosa looked at him for a long moment. Then she said, "Thank you, Daniel."

"Don't thank me. I should have known."

"You should have. But you did not. And now you do. We are going to leave it there, because we have a great deal to sign this morning, and I am not, at seventy-one, going to spend the morning forgiving you in detail when I can do it more efficiently in general. I forgive you in general. Sign your papers."

Daniel made the sound that was almost a laugh again, and this time it became, more or less, a laugh, and Lucia smiled, and Asha permitted herself, for the first time that morning, to feel something other than the careful neutrality she had been holding in front of her like a clipboard.

title: === SCENE 16 ===
content:
=== SCENE 16 ===
They worked through items six, seven, and eight. These were the items that did not require speeches: the disposition of the personal property, which Lucia and Daniel had divided over the weekend with a list that ran to two and a half pages and that contained, Asha noticed, a number of entries marked *to Rosa*, in Lucia's handwriting, against which Daniel had, at some point, written *agreed*; the resolution of the bank accounts, which were small and which would be closed by the end of the month; the filing of the final tax return, which Asha would prepare and which the siblings would sign in her office in early February. Each item took the time it took. No one rushed. No one stalled. Rosa poured coffee twice and then, when the pot was empty, made another pot, and when Daniel started to stand up to help her she waved him back into his chair and said, "Sit. You are signing things. I am making coffee. We are each doing what we are good at."

By twelve-thirty the documents were signed. Asha gathered the papers into the folders and the folders into her bag and stood up to stretch, and Lucia said, "Stay for lunch."

"I have a two o'clock."

"Then stay for thirty minutes. Rosa made soup yesterday. There is enough for four. There has been enough for four every day this week, which I think she has been doing on purpose."

"I have been doing it on purpose," Rosa said. "Sit down, Asha. The estate is closed. You are no longer billing us. You can have soup."

Asha sat down.

The soup was lentil, with carrots and a great deal of pepper, and there was bread that Rosa had bought, she said, from a bakery two blocks east which she had been buying bread from for thirty years and which she would, she said, continue to buy bread from for as long as her knees permitted the walk. They ate at the dining table, with the yellow pads pushed to one end and the pastry plate, now mostly empty, at the other. Daniel asked Lucia when she expected to list the New York apartment. Lucia said next month. Daniel said he could introduce her to someone, a friend of a friend, who knew the market in her neighborhood, and Lucia said all right, and Asha noticed that Daniel had offered her something useful without making it a transaction and that Lucia had accepted it without making it a debt, and she thought, eating her soup, that this was the actual deliverable of the work she had done in this house. Not the codicil. Not the schedule of payment. The fact that two people who had not known how to give each other small things were, over lentil soup, beginning to learn.

She did not say this. She ate her soup.

At one-fifteen she stood up. Rosa stood up with her and walked her to the door. In the hallway, where the light from the landing window came down warm on the floorboards, Rosa stopped her with a hand on her arm.

"Asha."

"Yes."

"You did this well."

"Thank you."

"I have seen a number of these. Most of them are done badly. This one was done well. I want to say it before you leave, because once you leave you are not coming back in any official capacity, and I do not like to leave true things unsaid."

"Thank you, Rosa."

"Will you come back in an unofficial capacity."

Asha looked at her. Rosa's face was steady and unsentimental and slightly amused, in the way that Asha had come, over two weeks, to recognize as Rosa's particular form of affection.

"I would like to," Asha said. "If it would not be an intrusion."
