"It would not be an intrusion. Lucia will want it. I will want it. Daniel, when he is being honest, will want it. Come for dinner some Sunday. Not next Sunday. The Sunday after. By then the house will have settled into being a house again and not a file, and we will be better company."

"The Sunday after next."

"Six o'clock. Do not bring wine. Lucia has enough wine. Bring nothing. Bring yourself."

"All right."

Rosa opened the door. Asha stepped out onto the stoop. The cold air was sharper than it had been at ten-forty, and the sun had moved further along the brick of the house across the street, and a woman was walking a small brown dog past the steps, and the woman nodded at Rosa in the doorway and Rosa nodded back, and Asha thought, this is a neighborhood, this is a block, this is a house on a block, and the people inside it are going to live here, and the work I did was a small piece of what made that possible, and that is enough. That is, in fact, more than enough. That is the work.

She walked to her two o'clock.

—

The Sunday after next was the first Sunday in February, and it snowed in the morning and then stopped, and by six the streets were wet and dark and the row houses on Spruce Street had their lamps on in their front rooms, and Asha walked up the steps and rang the bell and Lucia opened the door.

Lucia was wearing an apron. She had not been wearing an apron any of the previous times Asha had seen her, and the apron, which had a faded pattern of small blue flowers, was clearly not Lucia's. Asha did not ask. Lucia kissed her on the cheek, which she had also not done before, and said, "Come in, come in, Rosa is bullying me about the salt in the stew and I need a witness."

"I am not a witness anymore. I am a guest."

"Then come in as a guest and refuse to take sides."

The house smelled of stew and of bread and of a wood fire, which surprised her, because she had not registered, on any of her previous visits, that the house had a working fireplace. There was one, in the front parlor, and it was lit, and Daniel was sitting in front of it in an armchair that Asha recognized as having previously been in the back parlor, which suggested that some rearranging had been going on. He stood up when she came in.

"Asha."

"Daniel."

"I am glad you came."

"I am glad I came."

He had lost a little of the tightness around his eyes. Not all of it. Some of it, she suspected, would never leave, because some of it was older than this estate and older than his mother's death and older than the codicil, and a probate attorney was not in the business of fixing that kind of tightness. But some of it had gone, and what had replaced it was something that looked, in the firelight, like a man who had begun, tentatively, to consider the possibility that he might be liked by the people in the room without having to earn it that evening.

He poured her a glass of wine. She had not brought any, as instructed. The wine was good. They stood by the fire and talked about nothing in particular, which was a thing she had not done with Daniel before, because every previous conversation with Daniel had been about something in particular, and the particular thing had usually been a thing he wanted from her. Tonight he wanted nothing from her. He asked her about a case she had mentioned in passing two weeks ago and remembered the names of the parties, which she had not expected him to remember, and she found, talking to him, that the version of Daniel she was talking to was a version she could imagine being friends with, in the loose and undemanding sense in which the friend of one's sister's friend becomes, over years, a person one is glad to see.

Rosa came out of the kitchen and said dinner was ready and that the salt question had been resolved in her favor and that Lucia was sulking, and Lucia came out behind her and said she was not sulking, she was reserving judgment, and they sat down at the dining table, which had been set for four with the good plates, and the stew was excellent, and the bread was the bread from the bakery two blocks east, and the conversation moved, over the course of two hours, from the weather to a film Lucia was editing to a building Daniel's firm was working on to a story Rosa told about Mrs. Serrano in 1987 that none of the children had heard before and that made Lucia put down her fork and laugh and then, a moment later, cry a little, and then laugh again, and Daniel reached across the table and put his hand briefly on his sister's wrist, and Asha looked down at her plate, because there were moments in other people's families that one was permitted to witness but not to look at directly.

After dinner they moved back to the parlor. Rosa brought coffee. Daniel put another log on the fire. Lucia sat on the floor with her back against the couch, which Asha suspected was a position she had sat in, in this room, since she was a child, and which she had perhaps not been able to sit in for some weeks because the room had been too full of paperwork and grief and her brother. Tonight the room was full of none of those things. It was full of four people and a fire and the smell of coffee and the slow ticking of a clock on the mantel that Asha had not previously noticed.

At nine-thirty Asha said she should go. No one argued, which she appreciated, because the evening had reached the natural shape of its end, and it would have been a small unkindness to stretch it. Lucia got her coat. Daniel walked her to the door. Rosa, from the parlor, called, "Come again, Asha. Not as a project. As a person."

"I will."

"Good."

On the stoop Daniel paused. The snow had started again, very lightly, just enough to powder the railings.

"Asha."

"Yes."

"I was not easy."

"You were not."

"I know that. I want to say, for the record, that I know that. You handled me better than I deserved."

"I handled you as well as I could. You met me halfway. Eventually."

"Eventually."

"That is when most people meet anyone halfway, Daniel. Eventually is the standard. Earlier is the exception. You came in under the standard. That is what I would say if anyone asked."

He smiled, briefly. "Thank you."

"Good night, Daniel."

"Good night, Asha."

She walked down the steps and along Spruce Street toward the corner. At the corner she stopped and looked back. The row house stood between its neighbors with its front windows lit and its fire visible behind the curtain and the small powder of snow gathering on its railings, and inside it three people were doing the dishes and talking, and the house was, by any legal standard she could think of, settled, and by any other standard she could think of, beginning.

She turned the corner and went home.

—

title: === SCENE 17 ===
content:
=== SCENE 17 ===
She did not, that night, sleep badly. She slept the way she had used to sleep before the Serrano file had come into her office, which was not perfectly, because she was not a person who slept perfectly, but well enough. She woke at six. She made coffee. She sat at her kitchen table with a fresh pad of paper and a fresh pen and she wrote, at the top, the name of a new client, whose intake was scheduled for nine, and whose family, she had been told by the referring attorney, was difficult, and she underlined the word *difficult* and then, after a moment, crossed out the underline, because she had learned, over the last six weeks, that *difficult* was a word that estates threw at the people who handled them in order to scare them away from doing the work properly, and that the work, properly done, was almost always possible, and that the families who looked the most difficult from the outside were often the families who, on the inside, were most afraid that no one would help them tell the truth.

She drank her coffee. She walked to the office. She opened the new file.

—

The codicil, in its original form, with Rosa's signature on it as a witness and Mrs. Serrano's signature on it in the careful slow handwriting of a woman who had taken her time, was filed in the Register of Wills office in Philadelphia and assigned a number, and a copy of it was placed in the binder Asha kept for closed estates, and the binder was placed on a shelf in her office between two other binders of two other estates whose families had also, in their various ways, survived the process of settling what their dead had left behind.

The house on Spruce Street remained a house. Lucia lived in it. Rosa lived on the third floor. Daniel visited, at first awkwardly and then less awkwardly, on Sunday afternoons, and brought, by the spring, a woman he was seeing, who was kind to Rosa, which Lucia reported to Asha over coffee as the single most useful piece of information she had received about her brother in fifteen years. The charge on the property was paid down on the schedule Asha had drafted, and then, in the third year, paid off early, because Lucia's apartment in New York had sold for more than she had expected and because she found that she did not, in fact, miss it.

The letter Lucia had found in the sewing room, the one she had given to Asha and that Asha had given back to her, lived in a drawer in Lucia's bedroom, which had been her mother's bedroom, and Lucia read it, on the bad days, and put it back. She did not show it to Daniel. She did not need to. The letter had done its work in the moment it had been written and again in the moment it had been read, and what it had asked Lucia to do, Lucia had done, and the letter was now simply a piece of paper that her mother had once held in her hands and that, on the bad days, helped.

Rosa lived in the house for another nine years. She died in her sleep, in the third-floor room she had chosen, on a Tuesday in October, and Lucia found her in the morning and called Daniel and then called Asha, and Asha came over, not as the attorney, because Rosa had a different attorney by then, a friend of Asha's whom Asha had recommended when Rosa had decided, at seventy-five, to put her own affairs in order, but as a friend, and she sat in the kitchen with Lucia and Daniel and they drank coffee and waited for the people who had to come, and Lucia said, at one point, "She wanted to be here," and Daniel said, "She was here," and Asha said nothing, because there was nothing to say, and the kitchen was quiet, and the house was quiet, and outside on Spruce Street a woman walked a small brown dog past the steps, the same woman, or her daughter, or another woman entirely with another dog, it did not matter, because the block went on, and the house went on, and the people inside it, the ones still alive, went on, and that, Asha thought, sitting in the kitchen of a house she had once helped to keep from being sold, was what the work had been for.

She finished her coffee. She got up. She put her cup in the sink, the way Rosa had taught her, the first time she had ever stayed for lunch, by simply taking the cup out of her hand and rinsing it and setting it upside down on the rack and not saying anything about it, which had been Rosa's way of saying, *you are not a guest here anymore, you are a person, and persons rinse their cups.* She rinsed it now. She set it upside down on the rack.

Then she went back into the dining room, where Lucia and Daniel were sitting on the same side of the table, the way they had sat that Monday morning years ago, and she sat down across from them, at the place where she had sat the day they had closed the estate, and she waited with them, because waiting with people was, in the end, the largest part of what she did, and the part she had become, over a long career that had begun in earnest in this house, best at.

The clock on the mantel in the parlor ticked. The fire was not lit, because it was morning, and because no one had thought to lay one. The light from the landing window came down warm on the floorboards. The house held them, as it had held the woman who had built her family inside it and the woman who had kept that family running and the two children who had not always known what to do with either of them, and it would, Asha thought, hold them a while longer, which was all any house was ever asked to do, and all any of the people who worked on the paperwork of houses could ever, honestly, promise.

She sat with her friends and waited for the people who had to come.

Outside, the morning went on.
